analogy.p: A catalyst is like a **guide who knows a shortcut over a mountain**. Without the guide, hikers (reacting particles) must climb a very high pass (a high activation energy) and few make it in a day. The guide shows a lower route, so many more hikers reach the other side quickly, and the guide comes back unchanged to help the next group. The analogy also helps with the different charges: the guide can wear different 'outfits' (Fe2+ or Fe3+) as needed. It breaks down because the guide does not change where the hikers started or where they end up, but a real catalyst is a chemical that interacts with the reactants on its surface, and it may eventually be 'tired out' (poisoned) in practice.
analogy.t: A transition metal as a flexible tour guide

bullets: They occupy the **central block** of the periodic table, between the s-block metals (Groups 1 and 2) and the p-block elements (Groups 3 to 0).
Period 4 contains scandium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper and zinc; the block continues in periods 5 and 6.
All transition metals are **metals**, so they are found on the left and centre of the table, not with the non-metals.
They are not given a single group number in the AQA course because the block does not fit into the simple group numbering of 1, 2, 3 ... 0.
Their position explains why they differ from Group 1: they are further from the noble gases and have more complex electronic structures, which gives them different properties.
Typical exam question: 'State where in the periodic table transition metals are found' is answered: 'between Group 2 and Group 3 / in the central block'.
core.h: 1. Where the transition metals are in the periodic table
core.p: The **transition metals** are the block of metals found **between Group 2 and Group 3** of the periodic table, starting in **period 4** (the row beginning with potassium). They include familiar metals such as **iron, copper, nickel, chromium, manganese, titanium and cobalt**, as well as silver, gold, platinum and mercury further down. Because they sit in a block in the middle, the periodic table is wider in period 4 and below than in periods 1 to 3. The specification expects you to be able to locate them and to describe the properties that make them different from the Group 1 metals.

bullets: **Good conductors of electricity** because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge through the metal.
**Good conductors of heat** because delocalised electrons and vibrating ions pass energy through the lattice.
**Malleable and ductile** because layers of positive ions can slide over each other while the sea of electrons keeps holding them together.
**High density**: transition metals are generally heavy for their size; for example iron 7.9 g/cm3 and copper 9.0 g/cm3.
They are **strong and hard** compared with Group 1 metals, so they can be used for bridges, girders, engines and tools.
Most are **solid at room temperature**; the only common exception is **mercury**, which is a liquid at room temperature (melting point -39 C).
Combined with metallic bonding, this is why many transition metals are made into **alloys** such as steel (iron with carbon) and brass (copper with zinc).
core.p: Like all metals, transition metals have **metallic bonding**: a lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of **delocalised electrons**. This explains the general metal properties, which transition metals show strongly. They are **good conductors of heat and electricity**, **malleable** (can be hammered or bent into shape) and **ductile** (can be drawn into wires), and they are usually **shiny when polished**. They are strong enough and tough enough to be used in construction, tools and machines.

bullets: **Melting point:** transition metals have **high** melting points (iron 1538 C, copper 1085 C, nickel 1455 C, chromium 1907 C) whereas Group 1 metals have **low** ones (lithium 181 C, sodium 98 C, potassium 63 C). Mercury is the exception.

**Density:** transition metals are **dense** (about 7 to 9 g/cm3 for iron, nickel, copper); Group 1 metals are **low density** (lithium 0.53, sodium 0.97, potassium 0.86 g/cm3), and lithium, sodium and potassium float on water.
**Hardness and strength:** transition metals are **hard and strong**; Group 1 metals are **soft** and can be cut with a knife.

**Reactivity:** transition metals are **much less reactive**; they **do not react as vigorously with water or oxygen**. Group 1 metals react violently with water (2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2) and tarnish rapidly in air.
**Compounds:** transition metal compounds are often **coloured**; Group 1 compounds are usually white or colourless.
**Ions:** transition metals form ions with **different charges**; Group 1 metals always form 1+ ions.
**Catalysts:** transition metals and their compounds are **useful as catalysts**; Group 1 metals are not used for this.

The reason for the higher melting points and greater strength is stronger metallic bonding in transition metals (more electrons are delocalised, and the ions are held more tightly); do not give more detail than this at GCSE.
core.h: 3. Comparing transition metals with Group 1 metals
core.p: The specification asks for a **comparison with Group 1**, so you must be able to give pairs of facts. In short, transition metals are **harder, stronger, denser, have much higher melting points and are much less reactive** than the alkali metals. The Group 1 metals are soft enough to cut with a knife, float on water (lithium, sodium and potassium), melt at low temperatures and react vigorously. Using data in a table you should be able to decide which type a metal is from just a few numbers.

bullets: **Iron** reacts very slowly with air and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, which is **rust**; this needs both oxygen and water and is not a violent reaction.
**Copper** does not react with water or with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, but it slowly forms a green coating (copper carbonate) in damp air, the reason for the green colour of old roofs.
**Iron + dilute hydrochloric acid:** Fe + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2; the reaction is steady and slower than for Group 1 or Group 2 metals, and iron(II) chloride is produced.
**Sodium + water:** 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2 is rapid and exothermic; the contrast with iron, which barely reacts with cold water, is a standard exam comparison.

In the reactivity series, **iron** is below carbon, so it can be extracted by reduction with carbon (in the blast furnace), while the much more reactive Group 1 metals must be extracted by electrolysis.
Gold and platinum are so unreactive that they are found uncombined in nature, which is part of why they are valued for jewellery and electrical contacts.

Link to **corrosion:** iron needs protecting from rusting using paint, oil, galvanising or sacrificial protection, whereas Group 1 metals must be stored under oil to stop them reacting with air and water.
core.h: 4. Reactivity with water, oxygen and acids
core.p: Transition metals are **less reactive** than Group 1 metals, which can be seen from their reactions with water, oxygen and acids. Group 1 metals react at room temperature with cold water, producing hydrogen and a metal hydroxide. Most transition metals do not react with cold water at all, and some (such as copper, silver and gold) do not react with dilute acids either. When they do react, it is more slowly, and this connects with the **reactivity series** (iron and copper are below the Group 1 metals and Group 2 metals).

bullets: **Roman numeral = charge** on the metal ion: iron(II) means Fe2+ and iron(III) means Fe3+.
Examples: **FeCl2 is iron(II) chloride**, **FeCl3 is iron(III) chloride**, **FeO is iron(II) oxide**, **Fe2O3 is iron(III) oxide**, **CuO is copper(II) oxide**, **CuSO4 is copper(II) sulfate**.
To work out the formula from the name: iron(III) oxide has Fe3+ and O2-; for the charges to cancel you need **2 Fe3+ (6+) and 3 O2- (6-)** giving Fe2O3.
To work out the charge from the formula: in Fe2O3 the total negative charge is 3 × 2- = 6-, so each of the 2 iron ions is 3+, so the name is iron(III) oxide.
The charge shown by the Roman numeral is the same as the number of electrons lost by the atom: iron(III) means each iron atom has lost 3 electrons.
This property exists because transition metals can lose different numbers of electrons from their outer shells, and it is linked to why they can act as catalysts and form many coloured compounds.
Compare the metals in Groups 1 and 2, where the name does not need a numeral (sodium chloride, magnesium oxide) because only one ion is possible.
core.h: 5. Ions with different charges and the naming system
core.p: One distinctive property of the transition metals is that they can form **ions with different charges**. Iron, for example, forms both **Fe2+** and **Fe3+** ions, and copper can form Cu+ and Cu2+ (Cu2+ is by far the most common at GCSE). Group 1 metals always form 1+ ions and Group 2 metals always form 2+ ions, so this variable behaviour is a key difference. To tell the compounds apart, we use **Roman numerals in brackets** in the name to show the charge on the metal ion.

bullets: **Copper(II) compounds** such as copper(II) sulfate crystals and solutions are **blue**; copper(II) oxide is black.
**Iron(II) compounds** (Fe2+ solutions) are **pale green**; **iron(III) compounds** (Fe3+ solutions) are **yellow-brown/orange-brown**.
**Potassium manganate(VII)** (KMnO4) is **purple**; **potassium dichromate(VI)** is **orange**; **nickel(II)** compounds are **green**; **cobalt(II)** compounds are pink.
The same metal can give different colours with different charges, e.g. Fe2+ (pale green) and Fe3+ (yellow-brown), a reminder that charge changes the compound.

**Chemistry only (triple) link:** adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of a transition metal ion gives coloured hydroxide precipitates: Cu2+ → blue precipitate, Fe2+ → green precipitate, Fe3+ → brown precipitate.
Group 1 and Group 2 compounds are usually white or colourless (for example sodium chloride, magnesium oxide), so colour in a compound is a clue that a transition metal is present.
Exam tip: 'coloured compounds' is a property you give when asked to name a **property of transition metals compared with Group 1**.
core.p: Transition metal compounds are typically **coloured**, which is a major difference from Group 1 and Group 2 compounds (usually white or colourless). The colour of the compound depends on the metal and on its charge, so even two ions of the same metal can look different. These colours are very useful for identifying metal ions in chemical analysis, and they also give pigments for paints, glazes and stained glass.

bullets: **Iron** is the catalyst in the **Haber process** for making ammonia: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
**Nickel** is used as a catalyst in the **hydrogenation** of alkenes to make alkanes (and in making margarine from vegetable oils).
**Platinum** (and rhodium) are used in **catalytic converters** in car exhausts to speed up the conversion of carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
**Vanadium(V) oxide** is the catalyst in the Contact process for sulfuric acid (an example beyond the minimum GCSE list).
**Activation energy** is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react; a catalyst lowers this, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the rate increases.
On a **reaction profile** the catalysed pathway has a lower peak than the uncatalysed one but starts and ends at the same energy levels.
The catalyst is **not used up**, so it is not shown in the overall equation (it can be written above the arrow), and a small amount can be reused many times.
Catalysts are **specific**: a given catalyst works for particular reactions, which is why industry chooses carefully.
core.p: A **catalyst** is a substance that **speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up** in the reaction. Many transition metals and their compounds make good catalysts. A catalyst works by providing an **alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**, so more particles have enough energy to react when they collide. The overall energy change of the reaction (the energy of the reactants and products) is **not changed** by a catalyst, and the catalyst can be recovered chemically unchanged at the end.

bullets: **Lower temperature** means less energy is needed, which cuts costs and can reduce the burning of fossil fuels.
**Faster rate** means more product in a given time, so a smaller plant can produce more.
**Catalysts are not used up**, but they may become **poisoned** by impurities in the reactants and need replacing or regenerating.
Transition metal catalysts can be expensive (platinum, rhodium), so they are used as a thin layer on a ceramic honeycomb or as a **gauze** to give a **large surface area** with little metal.
A large surface area (powder, pellets, gauze) means more active sites for particles to collide with, so a faster rate.
Catalysts do **not change the position of equilibrium** in a reversible reaction (such as the Haber process); they only make the equilibrium be reached faster.
Evaluating questions: benefit = faster rate and lower energy cost; drawback = cost of the catalyst and the chance of catalyst poisoning.
core.p: In industry, catalysts make processes **cheaper, faster and more sustainable**. Because they lower the activation energy, reactions can run at **lower temperatures and pressures**, which saves energy and reduces fuel costs and carbon dioxide emissions. They also allow a reaction to reach the desired rate when otherwise it would be too slow to be economic. Because the catalyst is not used up it can be reused, which keeps the running costs down.

bullets: **Copper:** electrical wiring and water pipes, because it is an excellent electrical conductor, **ductile** (drawn into wires), malleable (bent to shape) and **unreactive** towards water.
**Iron / steel:** buildings, bridges, vehicles, because it is **strong, hard and cheap**; pure iron is soft so it is turned into steel (an alloy) for greater hardness.
**Titanium:** aircraft parts and replacement hip joints because it is **strong, low density for a transition metal** and resistant to corrosion.
**Platinum, gold:** jewellery and electrical contacts because they are very **unreactive** (do not corrode).
**Chromium:** chrome plating on car parts and taps because it forms a hard, shiny, corrosion-resistant coating.
**Nickel:** in alloys and coins, and as a catalyst.
Always include 'because' linking the property to its use, e.g. 'copper is used for wires because it is a good conductor and ductile'.
core.p: Examiners often ask you to **link a property to a use**. Transition metals are chosen because of specific properties. For example, copper is used for electrical wiring because it is a very good conductor and is ductile; iron (as steel) is used in construction because it is strong and cheap; and the high melting point of some transition metals allows them to be used for filaments and engine parts. Always state the property and say why it matters in that use.

bullets: **Low melting point (below about 200 C), low density (below 1 g/cm3), soft, reacts vigorously with water → Group 1.**
**High melting point (above 1000 C), high density (above about 7 g/cm3), hard, slow or no reaction with water → transition metal.**
**Coloured compounds or different oxidation states** also point to a transition metal.
**Evidence from reaction with water:** sodium reacts violently; if a metal shows no reaction with cold water, it is more likely to be a transition metal.
Mercury is the only liquid metal at room temperature, but it is still a transition metal with high density (13.5 g/cm3).
When answering, quote the **data values** from the table and say whether they match the usual pattern.
Compare like with like, e.g. 'metal X has melting point 1455 C which is much higher than sodium at 98 C, so X is a transition metal'.
core.h: 10. Data interpretation: deciding what type of metal
core.p: A common exam style gives a table of properties for several unnamed metals and asks you to say which are transition metals and which are Group 1 metals. You need to compare melting point, density, hardness and reactivity with the typical values. It helps to remember typical orders of magnitude: Group 1 metals melt below about 200 C and have a density below 1.0 g/cm3, whereas transition metals melt above about 1000 C and have densities of 7 g/cm3 or more.

bullets: **Metallic bonding:** explains why they conduct, are malleable and why alloying makes them harder.
**Reactivity series and extraction:** iron is extracted using carbon in a blast furnace; copper can be extracted by electrolysis or by smelting; unreactive metals can occur native.
**Rates of reaction:** catalysts lower activation energy and are shown on a reaction profile.
**Haber process:** iron catalyst, 450 C, 200 atmospheres; the catalyst speeds the reaction but does not change the yield.
**Chemical analysis (Chemistry only):** sodium hydroxide precipitates identify Cu2+ (blue), Fe2+ (green) and Fe3+ (brown) ions.
**Corrosion and alloys:** rusting of iron and the use of steel, stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel) and other alloys.
**Electrolysis and electroplating:** a thin layer of copper, nickel or chromium can be plated onto objects for protection or appearance.
core.p: This topic ties together **bonding, the reactivity series, rates of reaction, the Haber process, identification of ions and corrosion**. Showing a link between two parts of the course can improve an answer to extended response questions. It also helps you to explain why the same few metals appear in so many contexts: they are strong, versatile, and their compounds are colourful and catalytic.

exam: **1 mark:** state a property (e.g. 'form coloured compounds', 'high density') or the position ('between Group 2 and Group 3').
**2 mark comparison:** give a property of each type: 'Transition metals have higher melting points than Group 1 metals, and are denser'. Compare both, not just one.
**Use comparative words**: higher, harder, denser, less reactive; mark schemes need the comparison, not just 'high melting point'.
**Catalyst definition (2 marks):** 'speeds up the rate of reaction' and 'is not used up/is unchanged at the end'.
**Explain how a catalyst works (2-3 marks):** 'provides an alternative pathway', 'lower activation energy', 'more particles have enough energy / more successful collisions'.
**Name and formula questions:** use the Roman numeral to find the charge, then balance charges to get the formula (e.g. iron(III) oxide is Fe2O3).
**Reaction profile questions:** catalysed line has a lower peak; reactants and products at the same level; label activation energy as the arrow from reactants to the top of the peak.
**Industrial benefit (4 marks):** faster rate, lower temperature/pressure, less energy so lower costs, catalyst not used up; mention drawbacks like cost of platinum and poisoning.
**Data tables:** quote numbers and compare with Group 1 values (e.g. melting point 1455 C compared with 98 C for sodium).

**6 mark answer:** compare transition metals with Group 1 across at least three properties (melting point, density, strength, reactivity), then add colour of compounds, ions with different charges and catalysis.

mistakes.r: They are in the central block between Group 2 and Group 3; they are not given a single group number.
A catalyst is not used up; it is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction (though it can become poisoned in practice).
mistakes.w: A catalyst is used up and has to be replaced after the reaction.

mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; it does not supply energy.
mistakes.w: A catalyst provides energy for the reaction.

mistakes.r: Transition metals are much less reactive than Group 1 metals, even though they are harder and stronger.
mistakes.w: Transition metals are more reactive than Group 1 metals because they are stronger.

mistakes.r: The Roman numeral gives the charge: Fe2+ is iron(II) and Fe3+ is iron(III).
A catalyst speeds up the reaction but does not change the products, the position of equilibrium or the overall energy change.
mistakes.w: A catalyst changes the products or the overall energy change.

mistakes.r: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature; most others are solid.
mistakes.w: All transition metals are solid at room temperature.

mistakes.r: Group 1 compounds are usually white or colourless; coloured compounds are typical of transition metals.
mistakes.w: Group 1 compounds are coloured like transition metal compounds.

mistakes.r: They have high melting points and are hard, strong and dense, unlike Group 1 metals.
mistakes.w: Transition metals have low melting points and are soft.

summary: The spec asks you to know where the transition metals are in the periodic table and to compare their properties with Group 1 (higher melting points, density, strength and hardness, much lower reactivity), plus their ions with different charges, coloured compounds and use as catalysts. It matters because these properties explain why metals such as iron, copper and nickel are used in construction, industry and catalysis.

terms.d: A metal in the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3, with properties such as high density, high melting point, coloured compounds and catalytic behaviour.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up in the reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide in order to react.
A different route for a reaction with a lower activation energy, provided by a catalyst.
The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms that are free to move through the whole structure.
Able to be hammered or bent into shape without breaking.
Able to be drawn out into a wire.
A mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal; usually harder than the pure metal.
The mass of a substance in a given volume, measured in g/cm3.
A number in brackets after a metal's name showing the charge on its ion, e.g. iron(III) is Fe3+.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react together.
The industrial manufacture of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
A reaction in which hydrogen adds to a molecule such as an alkene; nickel is used as a catalyst.
A device in a car exhaust that uses platinum or rhodium catalyst to convert harmful gases into less harmful ones.
The destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with substances in the environment; rusting is the corrosion of iron.
A list of metals in order of how readily they react, used to predict reactions and extraction methods.

worked.ans: P is a Group 1 metal because it has a low melting point (63 C), low density (0.86 g/cm3) and reacts vigorously with cold water. Q is a transition metal because it has a high melting point (1455 C), high density (8.9 g/cm3), forms coloured compounds and does not react with cold water.
worked.q: The table gives data for two metals. Metal P: melting point 63 C, density 0.86 g/cm3, reacts violently with cold water. Metal Q: melting point 1455 C, density 8.9 g/cm3, forms green compounds, does not react with cold water. Identify the type of metal for each and justify your answers. [4 marks]
steps: Metal P has a **low melting point** and a **low density**, and reacts **violently with water**: this matches Group 1 (it is potassium).
Metal Q has a **high melting point** and **high density**, forms **coloured (green) compounds** and does **not** react with cold water: this matches a transition metal (it is nickel).
Compare with typical values: Group 1 metals melt below about 200 C; transition metals melt above about 1000 C.

worked.q: (a) Name the compound Fe2O3. (b) Write the formula of copper(II) chloride. (c) What is the charge on the iron ions in FeCl2? [3 marks]
steps: (a) Oxide ion is O2-. Three oxide ions give a total charge of 6-. So the two iron ions share 6+, i.e. 3+ each. The name is **iron(III) oxide**.
(b) Copper(II) means Cu2+. Chloride is Cl-. Two Cl- are needed to balance 2+, so the formula is **CuCl2**.
(c) Two chloride ions give a total of 2-. One iron ion balances this, so the charge is **2+** (iron(II) chloride).

worked.ans: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. More of the colliding particles have enough energy to react, so there are more successful collisions per second and the rate increases. The catalyst is not used up. In industry the iron catalyst means the reaction is fast enough at a lower temperature, saving energy and cost, and ammonia is produced more quickly; the catalyst can be reused.
worked.q: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process. Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction and give two advantages of using it in industry. [6 marks]
steps: State the definition: a catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up.
Explain the mechanism: it provides an **alternative pathway** with a **lower activation energy**.
Link to collisions: more particles have at least the activation energy, so **more collisions are successful** each second, so the rate increases.
Advantage 1: the process can run at a **lower temperature**, so less energy is used and costs are reduced.
Advantage 2: the reaction is **faster**, so more ammonia is made in a given time; the catalyst is not used up so it can be reused.
